text: Madness is a recurring theme in Celtic mythology. Figures who go mad often develop a prophetic or other paranormal skill. Male figures tend to go mad because of the horrors of war. Ancient Ireland called this soldier's heart, a state like what today we call post-traumatic stress disorder. The kings Suibhne and Muircertach Mac Erc both went mad from battle fatigue and died before they were fully healed. In Welsh mythology the warrior Myrddin, who becomes the magician Merlin in the Arthurian material, went mad from the horror of the battle of Arfderydd. He retreated to Scotland, where he both healed himself and discovered his prophetic powers. The link of madness to battle is reinforced by the Irish war goddess Nemain, whose name means war-frenzy. Female figures plagued with madness also appear. The most notable is Mess Buachalla. Her insanity came from her discovery that she had unwittingly committed incest with her father. Mis went mad after drinking her own father's blood. Even in such cases, madness typically results from violence or bloodshed.
objective: Document madness as a recurring Celtic mythological theme tied to battle and prophecy.
